notes: The case concerns municipal licensing of telegraph poles, not compensated occupancy of dwellings or rooms.

holding_summary: A tenant who abandoned leased premises remained liable under the lease unless the landlord’s agent had authority to accept the surrender. The scope of an agent’s authority when appointed orally was a question for the jury.

quotes.text: When a tenant abandons leased premises, with notice to the agent of the lessor who had collected the rent for the premises, ho will not be relieved from liability under the lease, unless it be shown that the agent had authority to accept a surrender.
On April 1,1886, defendant procured from plaintiff, as agent of his wife, a written lease for the premises for three years.

Now if you find such to be the case, that is, that Losch informed the agent of the landlord in 1887 that he would surrender up his lease and term, and did surrender it up and went out of possession, and paid the rent to the following April 1, 1888, that the agent of the landlord, acting within the scope of his authority, accepted such surrender and thereafter rented the property, or parts of it, and collected the rents for the estate of Murphy, or as agent of the landlord, then the defendant would thereby be released, and you should find a verdict in favor of the defendant, Losch.

notes: The premises included a portion in which the defendant lived and another portion that was sublet, but the record does not establish that the owner or original tenant fits the specified householder category.
The case construes a multi-year lease-option provision for unspecified premises and does not concern dwelling or room occupancy.

holding_summary: A landlord who permitted a tenant to sublet and agreed not to distrain the tenant’s personal property for the subtenant’s rent committed trespass by later distraining that property. Whether the landlord made the agreement was properly submitted to the jury.

quotes.text: If a landlord permits a tenant to sublet the demised premises, and agrees that the tenant’s personal property shall not be distrained for rent, he will bo a trespasser if he afterwards distrains.
Desiring to move west, he obtained permission from his landlord to sublet the demised premises to H. W. Harris.
The submission of this question was warranted by the evidence, and the verdict for plaintiff necessarily implies that the fact was found by the jury against the defendant.

notes: The tenant sublet a house while moving west; the facts indicate an anticipated occupancy of five or six months, but neither the landlord nor the sublessor is shown to be a resident householder.

holding_summary: The separate property of a tenant’s wife, when located in the leased family house, was subject to distress for unpaid rent. The Married Woman’s Act of 1848 did not change that landlord-and-tenant rule.

quotes.text: The goods of a tenant’s wife, found on the demised premises, are liable to distress for rent in arrear, though they are her separate property j the Married Woman’s Act of 1848 does not alter the law of landlord and tenant.
Louis Blanche leased a house in Sansom street, in Philadelphia, of Vincent L. Bradford, at an annual rental of $425, which he afterwards occupied with his family.

In fact she is no stranger to the lease, but one of the family for whom it was obtained, and therefore one of the tenants under it; her relation to her husband makes her so. She participates in the benefit of the lease, and there is no sufficient reason for saving her from liability for its burdens.

notes: The court recognized the wife as a tenant benefiting from the family house lease while also subjecting her separate goods to the lease’s rent burden; the landlord’s operating character is not stated.
